Title: Top 10 most overrated cards of the Jyhad

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
This is my measure of popular perceived usefulness vs. real, actual
usefulness. It's not that these are bad cards. It's just grating to
hear certain people drool mindlessly over them when they're only good
in specific circumstances. Read it, snarl at me, and have anger:

10) Rat's Warning - Unless you can defend it and punk him in combat. Even
then, he can just ignore it and take one whole pool per turn. How many
heavy animalism decks I've built that use one of these. Or none.

9) Telepathic Counter - It's a neat concept but it just doesn't do enough
for
a reaction card you have to hold in your hand until someone else takes an
action that allows you to use it. If it canceled 2/3 instead of 1/2, it
would be an interesting option (but the game has enough defense as it is).

8) Info Highway - For decks not built to take constant advantage of a fifth
and sixth transfer, it's benefit is entirely worthless unless it comes
up in the top 9 or 10 cards. Those are not good odds.

7) Delaying Tactics - If it's your only way to stop votes, I'd consider not
bothering with it and accepting the fact that if a critical votes comes
up,
you're screwed - because it doesn't actually stop them (usually), only
slows them down. (OK, I don't hate this card as much as I used to - it
does have _some_ value, even in the general case.)

6) Psyche! - You Psyche!, he S:CE's again. Oh, joy.

5) Sudden Reversal - Has uses against prey pool gain but if you're not a
quick
bleeding deck (or your prey doesn't have or doesn't draw his pool gain
cards), it's just you sacrificing your master phase for the benefit of the
rest of the table. Rather use my master phase to benefit me *alone*.

4) Recalled to the Founder - Sure it can put the hurt on someone - after
you've gotten two other event cards in play. You a trick shuffler?

3) Direct Intervention - Can save your butt if you're holding one at the
right
moment but most of the time, but a master phase plus a pool is too high a
price to be worthwhile most of the time.

2) Powerbase: Montreal - This is a card for weeny decks ("I'll trade action-
for-action between my weeny and your Leandro any day") and reaction
combat decks. It's other uses are...what other uses?

...and the most overrated card in Jyhad is:

1) Dreams of the Spinx - A short term high-speed Barrens. Other uses are
underwhelming.

+1 bleed vampires.
And finally, more cornercase, but I actually had this situation a couple
of times last sunday on ECQ, you don't have to bounce that bleed to
someone else, who will just bounce it to HIS prey.

2-cap.

it
> does have _some_ value, even in the general case.)

Delaying a Parity Shift after it has been Daring the Dawned and Awed is
actually pretty damn good. It surely stops them more often than not,
since it's the timed votes you need to delay. Sure, a KRC is usually not
worth delaying, but DU, Kindred Restructure or Parity Shift and
basically anything that has a requirement is good to delay. And, as said
before, it's a good way to get their vote pushers out of their hand.

> 6) Psyche! - You Psyche!, he S:CE's again. Oh, joy.

Psyche! does more than beat S:CE. It also given you new maneuvers on
weapons and replenishes everything that can be done "once per combat".
On top of that, you'll usually pack more Psyche! than he packs S:CE
simply because you can *always* play your Psyche's while S:CE is limited
to being in combat, which is generally not where decks that play S:CE
want to be.

> 5) Sudden Reversal - Has uses against prey pool gain but if you're not
a
> quick
> bleeding deck (or your prey doesn't have or doesn't draw his pool
gain
> cards), it's just you sacrificing your master phase for the benefit
of the
> rest of the table. Rather use my master phase to benefit me
*alone*.

These are a must-have in many decks. Suddening that Blood Doll or Minion
Tap is priceless. Or what about that Palla Grande or Week of Nightmares?
Gaint's Blood? A first turn Zillah's Valley or Info Highway?
If it gets into your hand at the right time it can mean the different
between no VP's and a tablewin.

> 4) Recalled to the Founder - Sure it can put the hurt on someone -
after
> you've gotten two other event cards in play. You a trick shuffler?

I think nobody rates this card as powerful. If you get it out (Storage
Annex, Fortschritt, what do you mean trick shuffler?) it's most likely
gonna screw up the table. It's more annoying than anything else. A
mistake to ever print, IMO. That said, I have a deck that uses it to
some effect.

> 3) Direct Intervention - Can save your butt if you're holding one at
the
> right
> moment but most of the time, but a master phase plus a pool is too
high a
> price to be worthwhile most of the time.

How is this not a good card? I saved my butt *MANY* times and I possess
only one. I always put it in any serious deck I build and I have never
regretted its inclusion. Mr. Potence is sitting on 6 red cards and a
Bum's Rush. DI the Bum's rush, and you're safe for a couple of turns.
Your Cailean is about to get royally screwed because you have a bad
hand. DI whatever is screwing him and he lives. DI a stealth card or a
conditioning that would oust your grandprey.
It's *one* pool. What action that's worth DI'ing costs you less than
that in resources? I actually DI'd a Approximation of Loyalty that
cancelled a bounce card played by my predator. Yeah, I took the bleed
for 6 myself and went on to sweep. Something I'd never manage with my
grandpredator at 6 extra pool.

> 2) Powerbase: Montreal - This is a card for weeny decks ("I'll trade
action-
> for-action between my weeny and your Leandro any day") and reaction
> combat decks. It's other uses are...what other uses?

It gains you a pool per turn? It can be stolen, sure. Which deck has
actions to spare to steal it constantly? The good thing about this is
that you get its benefit the same turn you gain control of it. The only
person you don't want to have it, is your prey. If your predator steals
it, good, that's one less action to hurt you. If someone crosstable
steals it, you can usually deal with him to ping pong it for a while.
Your predator is also unlikely to block your action stealing it from him
since he has more dangerous things to block. Say, his own predator. If
you're sitting with a wall deck somewhere, don't play it.

> ...and the most overrated card in Jyhad is:
>
> 1) Dreams of the Spinx - A short term high-speed Barrens. Other uses
are
> underwhelming.

You're kidding on this one right?

It's an accelerator, a cycler and a poolgainer. It's along with Bdoll
and DI in the Top 3 of best cards in VTES. I doubt someone will
disagree.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

Frederick Scott wrote:

> 10) Rat's Warning - Unless you can defend it and punk him in combat. Even
> then, he can just ignore it and take one whole pool per turn. How many
> heavy animalism decks I've built that use one of these. Or none.

I don't think I have ever heard anyone claim that Rat's Warning is
particularly good. I mean, if you are going to call something "overrated",
it should probably have at least been "rated" in the past...

I agree that it isn't that useful (90% of the time, you are better off with
a Wake or a Forced). But I don't think *anyone* thinks it is that useful.

>

Much like Rat's Warning, it isn't that useful, and I don't think anyone has
ever claimed it is.

>
> 8) Info Highway - For decks not built to take constant advantage of a fifth
> and sixth transfer, it's benefit is entirely worthless unless it comes
> up in the top 9 or 10 cards. Those are not good odds.

Ahh. Now here is a card that is claimed to be good by many, and as such,
could be called overrated. Agreed. It is a card that is really good if you
get it on the first turn. Meaning you need to have, like, 8 in your deck.

>
> 7) Delaying Tactics - If it's your only way to stop votes, I'd consider not
> bothering with it and accepting the fact that if a critical votes comes
> up,
> you're screwed - because it doesn't actually stop them (usually), only
> slows them down. (OK, I don't hate this card as much as I used to - it
> does have _some_ value, even in the general case.)

I don't think DT is overrated, as simply mentioned as a common base line
defense that is worth considering in most strategic decisions. It is never
the best anti vote option, but it is often one of the few viable anti vote
options, and as such, comes up a lot. I think I have one or two fringe
Delaying Tactics in pretty much every deck I own that doesn't have any other
significant vote defense (i.e. no inherrent vote lock or intercept). 'Cause
heck, even if you only stop the vote for a turn and it comes back the next
turn, keeping that 4 pool means you are alive an extra turn, which increases
your chances dramatically, or you keep your minion from getting PTOed for a
turn, at which point you can spitefully Rush the IC member, or most
importantly, you can stall the Dramatic Upheaval the turn before you oust
your prey, which is the turn voted "mostly likely for someone to play
Dramatic Upheval". Sure--other vote defenses are better (intercept, vote
power, whatever), but I'll still use a mini vote defense module of, like, 2
DT and a Vox Sennis (???--the vote trump OOT) in, like, all my Rush decks
and whatever. And DT is usually my last, best hope.

> 6) Psyche! - You Psyche!, he S:CE's again. Oh, joy.

Also a card that could arguably be called overrated. I don't think it is,
but then, I think it is good (and consequently, giving you reason to call it
overrated :-) Yeah, it is a 1 for 1 race (ya know, plus the other cards used
to hurt someone). But at least Celerity has the option of doing damage
without spending a lot of card up front (usually guns)--manuver with a gun,
stike with the gun, they Majesty, you Psyche. The card loss is comperable.
Yeah, it is 1 for 1 race of cards, but on the up side, the combat deck tends
to cycle faster, and consequently draw into Psyches faster than the non
combat deck draws in to Majesty. And the combat deck can usually afford to
pack more Psyches than the non combat deck can pack Majesties--if the
Majesty deck isn't sitting next to a Rush deck/blocker, those Majesties are
going to muck up your hand something fierce, where the Rush deck can always
cycle Psyches, even if it doesn't see a Majesty the whole game (to just
start combat over and shoot you again instead of, like, pressing or
additional striking). That, and Psyche is (much like Delaying Tactics) the
only real S:CE defense for a celerity based deck. So it is going to be used
a lot, regardless of whether or not it is actually that good (which I think
it is, but that is me).

> 5) Sudden Reversal - Has uses against prey pool gain but if you're not a
> quick
> bleeding deck (or your prey doesn't have or doesn't draw his pool gain
> cards), it's just you sacrificing your master phase for the benefit of the
> rest of the table. Rather use my master phase to benefit me *alone*.

Ahah! I agree! Completely! Yaa! Yeah. SR? The one of the most overrated
cards in the game (int he sense that it actually is rated as very useful by
many, many players, and I think it is mostly trash). Yeah, I too have built
S+B decks where every master slot is a Sudden Reversal, and that is kinda
useful. And yeah, I have been in gams where the game is won simply by
someone having a SR at the exact right moment. But the vast majority of the
time, SR sits in your hand, waiting for the right moment, and it inevitably
gets used on an Animalism master cross table, just to get it out of your
hand.

>
> 4) Recalled to the Founder - Sure it can put the hurt on someone - after
> you've gotten two other event cards in play. You a trick shuffler?

Yeah, this one, much like all the other "killer" events, are much scarier in
theory than in reality. Thay are really hard to get into play. And even
Recalled is easy to avoid. Sure, *if* it hits the hable and *if* you are
playing a very clan focused deck, it'll hose you. But those are two big
"if"s.

>
> 3) Direct Intervention - Can save your butt if you're holding one at the
> right
> moment but most of the time, but a master phase plus a pool is too high a
> price to be worthwhile most of the time.

Also agreed. Much like SR, sooooo very randomly reactive. Occasionally,
it'll win you the game. Most of the time, not so much.

>
> 2) Powerbase: Montreal - This is a card for weeny decks ("I'll trade action-
> for-action between my weeny and your Leandro any day") and reaction
> combat decks. It's other uses are...what other uses?

Eh. I'd never claim that it is gonna, like, win you games, but it'll never
hurt you to put in your deck--it is free pool, possibly a lot of free pool.
And it is free pool you can give to someone who needs free pool.

>
> ...and the most overrated card in Jyhad is:
>
> 1) Dreams of the Spinx - A short term high-speed Barrens. Other uses are
> underwhelming.

It doesn't *need* any other uses. The other uses (use?) are pure gravy. It
is the *best* hand cycler in the game (The Barrens and Nod are both
incredibly common, as hand cycling is incredibly good, and as a cycler, it
is better than both of those) *and* it can, in a pinch, give you pool and
transfers. At the very least, it can pay for itself.

Unlike the other cards above that I agree are overrated (in the sense that
many folks seem to think they are really useful, but I tend to think not so
much), Dreams has *zero* down side. It doesn't clog your hand waiting for
the right moment. It is always proactively useful. It is usually free. If
you get it early, it speeds up your early game. If you get it mid game, it
gives you unprecidented hand cycling ability. If you get it late game, it
can get you some vital precious pool *or* cycle in a pinch. I'd never claim
that Dreams will win you the game just by being in your hand (although I
have many times won a game 'cause Dreams was in my hand...), but it is a
card with zero downside and many, many upsides. As I have argued about the
card many times, it doesn't have such a earth shattering effect that it
needs to be fixed/changed/tweaked/whatever. But it is a fantastic card that
is always good to have.

Especially Sudden Reversal. I try to play with it occasionally, only

least, not unless it's you and him.

Overrated only until the whole Gehenna thing finally blows over.

If you're intercept+combat, there is no better pool gain master.

> 1) Dreams of the Spinx - A short term high-speed Barrens. Other uses are

I would much like to argue with that description.

From your post:

> It's just grating to hear certain people drool mindlessly over
> them when they're only good in specific circumstances.

I would contend that "only good in specific circumstances" applies to
DotS LESS than it does to any other card in the ENTIRE GAME.

The Barrens is really quite good. A "high-speed Barrens" sounds even
better. And Dreams is such, only if and when you want it to be. You
could also call it a "way-improved Deal with the Devil", since after
replacing itself and being used 3 times you've got (1+2+2+2)=7 cards,
and you got to draw first instead of discard first. It is not "short
term" because 2 plays of Dreams = 6 turns. Given average game length
seems to be 12--15 turns, 6 turns is just under half, and being in
play for half of the game != "short-term".

I don't think there is better hand-cycling, unless you can protect
Fragment (or really mack it with Servitor of Irad. :) Everything else
seems to be one-shot or one-at-a-time.

Where the number is written as "# of pool you would gain if you
maximized pool retrieval from this card up to that point" and it is
assumed that any (D) actions at a card were unsuccessful.

Looking at 5 turns in play,
(This assumes you'll get 5 turns on average out of a poolgain master)

Meaning that DotS is as good a bet as any for pool gain (save

So if you can't spare three more MPA's or a vampire, you don't want
random pool gain, and you can't count on protecting a location, this
is what you're left with.

Presumably Dreams is used in so many decks not just to speed up
influence, not just to draw a whole new hand (replace Dreams + draw 6
= 7 cards), but to Gain 2 Pool!

After all, there are remarkably few options to gain pool via master
cards, and actions can be blocked.

In conclusion:

Dreams is in the mid-range of master-card pool gain.
Dreams is on the Very Top of card cycling.
Dreams is on the Very Top of versatility.
Therefore, Dreams is VERY hard to overrate.

I own at least 13 copies of Dreams of the Sphinx.
I am planning on having over 30 decks.
I do not like switching cards between two or more decks.
It follows that I am planning on having around 40 copies of Dreams.
Current distribution of Dreams makes this expectation either
unrealistic or cost-prohibitive.

I would like to see Dreams made common.
If a player is likely to have 3 Blood Doll and 2 Dreams in a
Tournament-Winning Deck, why do 3 Blood Dolls come in a starter deck,
and no Dreams?
Alternately, if Dreams were only usable twice...

Eh.
In the meanwhile, please trade me all your Dreams.

-- Brian

>in specific circumstances. Read it, snarl at me, and have anger:

Measuring overratedness is a challenging endeavor, isn't it? I think the
easiest is to compare personal valuations to people around you. When trying to
gauge stranger valuations, it's hard to pinpoint just how strongly they feel
about a card. Of course, when people constantly say "this is one of the top 3
cards in the game", there's something to work with. Then, perceptions change
constantly and the game itself changes every once in a while.

Having said that, if I had to pare down to a 10 card list of what I felt people
overrated the most, it would be something like (in alphabetical order, ignoring
Gehenna):

Art Scam
Disarm
Gather
Khobar Towers
Read the Winds
Skin of Rock
Tribute to the Master
Visit from the Capuchin
Year of Fortune
Zillah's Valley

Out of the cards you mentioned, I'd consider PB: Montreal. I tried to
eliminate cards that were really bad that people thought weren't really bad,
i.e. tried to come up with cards that either were okay but thought of as
particularly good or were even good but were thought of as OMG!. Just to get
people to focus on the difference between saying something is overrated and
saying something isn't good, for instance, I see Read the Winds as a good card
but not up to the hype. I suppose it's not terribly useful to people to just
list the cards without any explanation, but I want to try to cut down on *some*
of the verbiage and I still see this thread being Fred's show.

>8) Info Highway - For decks not built to take constant advantage of a fifth
> and sixth transfer, it's benefit is entirely worthless unless it comes
> up in the top 9 or 10 cards. Those are not good odds.

I'm not sure what suggests people overrate this. I don't see people make a big
deal of playing it. If anything, right this moment, I'd be thinking people
underrated it. Certainly, our valuations of it (and other cards) color views.
I see Info Highway often having uses in the mid or endgame and being the most
powerful first turn play in the game.

>6) Psyche! - You Psyche!, he S:CE's again. Oh, joy.

I think people overrate Celerity as a whole, but without Psyche!, why would
anyone play Celerity combat (without support from things like T. Tracking or
Grapple) given that combat ends would always defeat it?

As I said, PB: Montreal is the only one on your list that might make mine.
And, having seen it in fewer decklists and fewer "you should play this"
comments, I'm not so sure it would mark.

What we could use, though, is probably an underrated thread. T10 overrated
isn't likely to stimulate deckbuilding creativity whereas T10 underrated may.
But, it might be a real pain to come up with a well-organized list.

'Cause, in general, it is a hard and fast rule. I mean, yeah, you could
certainly argue that it would be ok to build vampires completely arbitrarily
(i.e. there being no relationship at all between the size of the vampire and
thenumber of abilities) and it wouldn't destroy the game. But that isn't how
the game works currently. Nor is it ever how that game has worked. Vampires
have always been designed such that there is a direct relationship between
capacity and abilities. Ian Forrestal completely ignore this relationship.
If you are going to have rules, you might as well follow them.

better that the current design team chose to leave Ian Forrestal (which the
current design team didn't design, mind you) as a freak outlier rather than
using him as an excuse to make lots of other vampires that completely ignore
the existing design rules.

Vampire design follows hard and fast rules. And it still does. Ian is a
freak outlier. And seeing how the vast majority of the vampires printed
since SW have followed the hard and fast rule, it is reasonable to think
that the designers want to continue to follow that hard and fast rule.

> > Chicago -1 -1 0 1 2 3 4 5
>

I did not take it off every other turn. Each entry shows pool gain if
Pb:C gains a counter every turn, then the pool is all taken off on the
turn corresponding with that entry.

Turn 1, player must have lost 1 pool. (-1)
Turn 2, player puts one on, but has been unable to gain any yet. (-1)
Turn 3, player may have put one on and taken it off. (0)
Turn 4, player may have put on twice and taken them off. (+1)
Turn 5, player may have put on thrice and taken them off. (+2)
Turn 6, player may have put on four times and taken them off (+3)

I would not take off every other turn; I would maximize pool gain for
each turn separately. The chart of how much pool you can gain was not
intended to be linear.

> > Washington: D.C. -1 -1 0 1 2 2 3 4
>
> Why put only 1 on it?

Turn 1, only possible return is "paid 1 pool." (-1)
Turn 2, best possible return is to not put counters on. (-1)
Turn 3, best return is put 1 pool on, and take two counters off. (0)
Turn 4, best return is put 2 pool on, and take four counters off. (1)
Turn 5, best return is put 3 pool on, and take six counters off. (2)
Turn 6, best return is still put 3 on, take 6 off. (2)
Turn 7, best return is just like turn 5, plus put 1 pool on and take 2
off. (3)

I hope you understand what I am doing here.
Turn 4 (above) and Turn 5 (above) cannot coexist. You must choose one
or the other. Each one maximizes Pb:WDC's pool gain for that turn,
but not for any of the others.

A chart of Powerbase: Washington, D.C.'s pool change when taken to be
both linear and long-term would read:

W, D.C. -1 -4 -2 0 2 -1 1 3 5 2

Choppy and crappy and clear why nobody uses Pb:WDC -- Because even at
turn 10, you've only gained 2 pool.

>

Getting the pool gains listed above to come out in the /order/ listed
would be impossible for some of the cards. I only intended to
maximize pool [for each entry], not [for each entry given previous
entry states were all passed through]

> Next, I don't see a fast forward moving deck as benefiting from

I guess I have a completely different way of seeing it. Again,
this hinges on the point that if you hover _near_ an early oust,
the table will turn against you trying to prevent it and your
prey will turn backwards trying to survive. I usually see defense
as what you usually give up to get all the offense for the quick
kill. So having a prey get off even one Minion Tap could be the
difference between sweep-the-table and being ousted. It's long
slow decks that shouldn't bother trying to stop bloat - you're
NOT going to stop all of your opponents from bloating over the
course of the game.

>The deck that creeps forward towards its first VP and then
>collapses the three way would benefit far more by Suddening
>pool gain, for example.

Don't think so. Obviously, you're not going to oust anyone in
"slow motion". You might chip off their pool a bit until they're
within range and then suddenly tap out trying to oust. Against
bloat, you wind up hoping they spend themselves within range since
you're just not going to bleed them anywhere near death yourself,
even with SRs. And I don't know why you'd expect to collapse
the three-way after that, since all your master card power has been
concentrated on the guy who's out of the game.

But usually, I think of a slow deck as something that's building
its own power over time. Playing one-against-three or one-against-
four by cancel other peoples' masters with your masters is a losing
game.

Fred
